title: Corrosion depth under two coatings
intro:
Steel panels were coated by two processes and put through 500 hours of salt spray. The pit depth (µm) was measured on 9 panels from process 1 and 12 from process 2. Does the mean pit depth differ between the processes? Test H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 against H₁: μ₁ − μ₂ ≠ 0 at α = 0.05 with **Welch's t-test** (the samples are independent and you have no reason to assume equal variances).

Find the t statistic, the Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom and the two-sided p-value. Give t and df to two decimals and p to three decimals or more.

To use the Workbench: press **Copy the data**, press Ctrl+B, click **+ Data table** and paste (Ctrl+V). Choose **Two-sample test**, set **Test** to *Two means, unequal variances (Welch t)*, **Data from** to *Columns of a data table*, **Column (sample 1)** to *Process 1*, **Column (sample 2)** to *Process 2*, **Alternative hypothesis** to *Two-sided (≠)*, **Significance level (α)** to 0.05 and **Hypothesised difference (Δ₀)** to 0. Ctrl+L brings you back.

Statistic.says: That is the pooled t, which assumes equal variances. Welch keeps them apart: SE = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).
Check the sign. t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/SE with process 1 first, and process 1 has the smaller mean, so t is negative.

DegreesOfFreedom.says: n₁ + n₂ − 2 = 19 belongs to the pooled test. Welch's ν comes from the Welch–Satterthwaite formula.
min(n₁, n₂) − 1 = 8 is the conservative shortcut some textbooks allow. This exercise asks the Welch–Satterthwaite ν.

PValue.says: That is a one-tailed p-value. H₁ is two-sided (≠), so p = 2 × P(T > |t|).
That is the pooled test's p-value (19 df). Use Welch's t and its ν.

hints: First the summaries: x̄₁, s₁ and n₁ = 9 for process 1; x̄₂, s₂ and n₂ = 12 for process 2 (s with n − 1).

ν = (a + b)² / (a²/(n₁ − 1) + b²/(n₂ − 1)) with a = s₁²/n₁ and b = s₂²/n₂. Then p = 2 × P(T > |t|) with ν degrees of freedom: Python 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t), nu), R 2 * pt(abs(t), nu, lower.tail = FALSE).
